b: Everyone procrastinates now and then, but it’s not usually that much of a problem. The perennial procrastinator might be a different story. Peggy is constantly putting things on her to-do list that she never actually does, or at least not when she says she will. Her kitchen has a small pile of gadgets, receipts, and empty bottles that she keeps promising to clean out but hasn’t gotten to it. It’s annoying, but not as bad as the problems she’s creating with her friends, who have all but given up on her showing up when she says she will whether for a dinner, a show, or just a friendly get-together.

Peggy would like to change, but she’s stuck on how to get out of her rut. She also worries, in the back of her mind, that this chronic lateness could eventually erode her relationships, if not the tidiness of her home.
Perennial Procrastination as a Personality Trait

Within personality theory, procrastination becomes not just an annoying habit, but potentially a trait or enduring disposition. According to Durham (UK) University’s Fuschia Sirois and Cormac Monaghan (2026), this trait receives the condemning definition of “a form of chronic self-regulation failure involving the unnecessary and voluntary delay of important intended tasks despite knowing that negative consequences may result."

The idea that people who procrastinate can’t self-regulate takes on greater impact when, as the authors point out, this trait contributes to poor health. Oddly enough, not only can procrastination create negative health consequences, it may be precisely within the realm of health that procrastinators commit their most serious problems.

There is plenty of evidence, the Durham U. researchers suggest, for the risk presented by procrastination to various health domains, such as sleep problems, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease. The procrastinator most likely encounters these problems by putting off bedtime, going to the gym, or starting to eat a more healthy diet. But what about a person’s overall levels of health-related well-being? Called “self-rated health” (SRH), Sirois and Monaghan propose that it is precisely the nature of procrastination that should relate to lower SRH because procrastinators, according to other research, tend to experience an undue amount of negative affectivity or unhappiness.

Then there’s the concept of future SRH (FSRH). Because they tend to deny, compartmentalize, and avoid dealing with things that are bad, procrastinators may, oddly enough, rate their FSRH as higher than their current SRH.
They think, in other words, that their current problems will magically disappear.

The key factor linking procrastination with poor SRH and potentially higher FSRH, the authors propose, is stress. Procrastinators can get just as angry at themselves as can their friends and family. They can ruminate over their chronic lateness, putting a strain on their ability to keep their immune system functioning optimally. Poor SRH would reflect the toll that constant lateness (and rumination over lateness) takes on a procrastinator’s physical health.
Testing Procrastination’s Effect on Self-Rated Health

Using a large set of independent samples (from a total of over 8600 participants), the Durham U. researchers tested their model in which trait procrastination influences SRH and FSRH through the intermediary of perceived stress. Items measuring procrastination included “I often find myself performing tasks that I had intended to do days before,” and “I often think that I don’t get things done on time.” Perceived stress was assessed with items such as “In the last month, how often have you felt that you were unable to control the important things in your life?” A 36-item health questionnaire asked participants to rate their current health on a 5-point scale. FSRH was measured with the same questionnaire but as participants anticipated they would be 10 years in the future.

The final model supported the initial predictions that stress would play a role in the procrastination-health link. Poor SRH was predicted by chronic procrastination in a direct manner as well as through the route of perceived stress.

Breaking this down, the anxiety and depression associated with trait procrastination activates physiological arousal, becoming its own source of symptoms. Perceived stress, additionally, adds a cognitive component to chronic stress activation, affecting overall health appraisals and expectations of poor future health.

The story was somewhat more complex for FSRH. There was, as the authors anticipated, a certain denial factor associated with procrastination. Not all procrastinators saw their future health as suffering, although slightly more men did than women. It appeared that “optimistic views of health improving in the next 10 years may be fuelled in part by the difficulties in future-oriented thinking associated with chronic procrastination." In other words, procrastinators simply don’t think about the future; hence their inability to plan for it.
Overcoming the Procrastination Effect on Your Health

Even if you’re not the kind of procrastinator that Betty is, there are likely times in your life when you would rather not deal with something unpleasant involving your health. Who wants to take time out of their busy schedules to sit in a physician’s waiting room to get an annual check-up, to get lab work done, or to sit in a dentist’s chair for an hour or more?

Looking at the cognitive aspect, or stress part, of the equation, you can also see how dealing with the worry and distress the procrastination adds to your life can contribute to a poor overall sense of well-being. What’s more, thinking about how ineffective you are by not doing what you’re supposed to can spiral into added heaps of stress.

Turning your procrastination around may not be that easy. This is especially challenging if your procrastination includes unrealistically imagining that the future will be better than the present. Taking a page from the cognitive stress model, use problem-focused coping, in which you get started on tackling the most manageable tasks first. By seeing yourself as successful in accomplishing small feats of timeliness, you can build the confidence that the bigger ones can also be tackled in time.
To sum up, knowing that procrastination has these negative consequences can help firm your resolve to regulate your time in a way that will help you build to a healthier future.
Not all procrastination is bad, though: See my previous post detailing some of its benefits for creativity.
